title: AI-Powered Humanoid Robot 'Sally' to Teach New York Students — But Its Maker's Past Raises Eyebrows
excerpt: Salamanca City Central School District in Western New York will deploy a $57,590 humanoid robot built by Realbotix, a company with roots in the adult entertainment industry, to teach STEM to 500 high school students this fall.
body:
• Salamanca City Central School District in Western New York will deploy an AI-powered humanoid robot named Sally to assist with STEM instruction for approximately 500 high school students starting this fall.
  • The robot costs $57,590 — discounted from $95,000 — and is built by Realbotix, a company whose parent acquired adult entertainment doll maker Abyss Creations in 2024, drawing sharp criticism.
  • Sally will operate on an offline, closed AI system, will not collect personal data or record audio/video, and is designed to supplement — not replace — human teachers.
  • The pilot marks the first deployment of a humanoid robot in a U.S. public school classroom.

A small school district in Western New York is about to become the testing ground for what could be a landmark experiment in American education — or, depending on whom you ask, a cautionary tale about the rush to inject artificial intelligence into classrooms.

Salamanca City Central School District, located on the Seneca Nation's Allegany Indian Reservation in Cattaraugus County, roughly 60 miles south of Buffalo, will deploy an AI-powered humanoid robot named Sally to assist with teaching STEM subjects to 11th and 12th grade students beginning this fall. The district currently enrolls approximately 1,400 students, with over 32% identifying as American Indian.

https://x.com/NDTVWorld/status/2079044638766415884

The robot is being built by Realbotix Corporation (TSX-V: XBOT), a Las Vegas-headquartered developer of humanoid robots and AI systems, as part of its Optio AI teaching assistant initiative. Sally will first assist with Salamanca's summer programs and STEM camps before expanding to roughly 500 high school students in September 2026.

What Sally Can Do — and What She Can't

Sally is designed to resemble a human, standing 5 feet 8 inches tall with silicone skin, and is capable of facial expressions, upper-body movements, and natural language conversation in more than 100 languages. However, she will remain seated in the classroom and cannot move independently.

Students will log in using unique ID numbers, allowing Sally to track their learning history and continue discussions from earlier sessions. An online avatar version of the AI will also be available around the clock for homework support.

"It's designed to give you answers and make things in life simpler and faster. But that is sort of the opposite of what we want to do in school, which is teach students how to solve problems," Superintendent Mark Beehler told the Buffalo News. He said the district has worked with Realbotix to "dial back" many of the AI's shortcut-oriented features and turn it into a teaching tool that prompts students to think for themselves rather than providing direct answers.

The district has emphasized that Sally operates on an offline, closed AI system, will not use facial recognition, will not record audio or video, and will not transmit data to Realbotix. "The Realbotix educational robot will never replace teachers, staff members, or meaningful human interaction," the district said in a statement.

The Controversy: From Sex Dolls to Schoolrooms

The deployment has drawn intense scrutiny because of Realbotix's corporate lineage. The company was previously known as Tokens.com, a Toronto-based cryptocurrency firm, before rebranding in May 2024 — one month after acquiring Simulacra Corporation, the parent company of Abyss Creations, a manufacturer of high-end adult entertainment dolls marketed under the RealDoll brand.

Critics, including outlets like Gizmodo and Kotaku, have questioned why a company with roots in adult products is now building teaching robots for children. The optics have been further complicated by Realbotix's website, which lists "Companionship" as a use case for its robots, describing them as tools to "tackle North America's staggering loneliness epidemic."

Realbotix has pushed back forcefully. In a statement, the company said the Salamanca robot is "a new unit" being built at Realbotix LLC's manufacturing facility, with "no RealDoll employees, blueprints, designs, products or technology involved." It emphasized: "The Salamanca robot is not anatomically correct and has never been designed, manufactured, marketed, sold or used as an adult product."

There are also questions about cost. The district paid $57,590 — described as a discount from the $95,000 list price — in a community where the median household income is $30,996 and 22.2% of the population lives below the poverty line, according to census data cited by New York Focus.

What It Means for Indian-American Families

For the Indian diaspora in the United States — which has among the highest rates of STEM employment and places enormous emphasis on educational quality — the Salamanca pilot raises pointed questions. If AI teaching assistants prove effective, they could democratize access to personalized tutoring for students who cannot afford private tutors, a prospect that resonates in communities where education is viewed as the primary vehicle for upward mobility.

Conversely, the experiment underscores growing anxieties about AI displacing skilled professionals, including educators. Indian-American tech workers are disproportionately represented in the AI and robotics sectors building these very tools, creating a complex dynamic where the community is both architect and potential subject of disruption.

What Happens Next

Realbotix CEO Andrew Kiguel has described the Salamanca deployment as a "flagship" pilot and "the beginning of a new era where humanoid robots and intelligent AI assistants become standard tools in STEM education." The company anticipates expanding beyond Salamanca if the pilot succeeds.

For now, the eyes of education technology watchers — and skeptics — will be on a small district in Western New York, where 500 students are about to meet their new classmate.
